title: Security Operations
intro:
Domain 4 is the largest slice of the SY0-701 exam at 28 percent, and it is the domain that looks most like the actual job of a SOC analyst. Where Domain 1 and Domain 2 are about concepts and threats, Domain 4 is about doing: hardening a server before it goes live, running a vulnerability scan and deciding which findings matter, reading a SIEM alert, tuning out the noise, responding to an incident, pulling logs for an investigation, managing identities and access, and running the automation and awareness programs that keep all of that sustainable. If you want to be hired into a SOC at a Nigerian bank or fintech, this domain is the one your interviewers will probe hardest, because it maps directly onto tier-1 and tier-2 analyst tasks.

The domain has nine objectives. This first half covers 4.1 through 4.4: applying security techniques to computing resources (baselines, hardening, wireless, mobile, application security), asset management across the whole lifecycle, vulnerability management from identification through remediation and reporting, and the alerting and monitoring stack (SIEM, SCAP, NetFlow, DLP, antivirus, SNMP). The second half covers firewalls and secure protocols, identity and access management, automation, incident response and digital forensics, and data sources for investigations.

Study advice: this domain rewards understanding process, not memorising lists. For every topic ask three questions. Why does this control exist, what does it look like when it is done well, and what would I actually do with it on a Monday morning in a SOC? The exam loves scenario questions here: it describes a situation and asks for the BEST next step or the MOST likely cause. Practise reading a CVSS vector, practise deciding whether a scan finding is a false positive, practise ordering the steps of vulnerability remediation, and you will find these questions become predictable.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources

videos.title: Secure Baselines
videos.summary: Messer explains what a security baseline is, where baselines come from (vendors, CIS, DISA STIGs), and the three-stage lifecycle of establishing, deploying and maintaining them.
videos.deepDive:
A secure baseline is a documented, agreed minimum configuration for a type of system: every setting, service, patch level and permission that must be true before that system is considered safe to run. The point is consistency. If you have 400 Windows servers and each was configured by whoever built it that week, you do not have 400 servers, you have 400 unique risks. A baseline turns them into one known configuration that can be tested once and enforced everywhere.

The SY0-701 objective breaks the baseline lifecycle into three activities, and the exam expects you to know them in order.

  1. Establish. Decide what the baseline is. You rarely start from a blank page. The usual sources are vendor hardening guides (Microsoft Security Baselines, Cisco hardening guides), the CIS Benchmarks (Center for Internet Security, free, hundreds of pages per platform, with Level 1 for general use and Level 2 for high-security environments), and the DISA STIGs used by the US Department of Defense. Your organisation then tailors these: a CIS rule that disables SMBv1 is kept, a rule that breaks your core banking middleware gets a documented exception. The result is written down and version-controlled.
  2. Deploy. Push the baseline out in a way that does not depend on humans remembering things. On Windows that is Group Policy or Intune; on Linux it is Ansible, Puppet or Chef; in the cloud it is infrastructure-as-code (Terraform modules, AWS Config rules) and golden images. A golden image is a pre-hardened virtual machine or container template, so every new instance starts compliant rather than being fixed afterwards.
  3. Maintain. Configurations drift. An admin opens a port to debug a problem and forgets to close it; a patch resets a registry key; a new CVE means a previously acceptable setting is now dangerous. Maintenance means continuous compliance scanning against the baseline (Nessus and Qualys both have CIS policy audit modes, and SCAP-based tools do the same), alerting on drift, and a change-control process for updating the baseline itself.

Worked example. A fintech in Lagos builds a new Ubuntu 22.04 API server. The baseline (derived from CIS Ubuntu Level 1) says: SSH root login disabled, password authentication off in favour of keys, auditd enabled, unattended-upgrades on, only ports 22 and 443 listening, ufw default deny inbound. The Ansible playbook applies all of that on first boot. Three weeks later a Nessus compliance scan flags that PermitRootLogin is now yes. That is drift. The SOC raises a ticket, the change is traced to an engineer who was troubleshooting and never reverted it, the playbook is re-run, and the incident is logged as a configuration-management failure rather than a breach.

Why the SOC cares. Baselines are what make anomaly detection possible. If you know every workstation should have Defender running and PowerShell logging enabled, then a host where those are off is immediately interesting. Baselines also make audit easier: when the CBN or an ISO 27001 auditor asks how you know your servers are hardened, the answer is a baseline document plus scan evidence, not a promise.

Do not confuse a baseline with a benchmark. A benchmark (CIS, STIG) is the published external reference. A baseline is your organisation's adopted, tailored version of it. The exam may use the terms loosely, but if a question asks about an industry-published standard the answer is benchmark; if it asks about your organisation's required configuration the answer is baseline.

keyTerms.def: The documented minimum security configuration an organisation requires for a class of system before it is allowed into production.
A free, consensus-developed hardening guide from the Center for Internet Security, published per platform with Level 1 and Level 2 profiles.
Security Technical Implementation Guide, a detailed hardening standard published by the US DISA and widely used as a baseline source.
A pre-hardened, pre-approved system or container image used as the template for all new deployments so they start compliant.
The gradual divergence of a live system from its approved baseline through untracked changes, patches or troubleshooting.
A scan that compares a system's actual configuration against a baseline or benchmark policy rather than looking for vulnerabilities.
Defining servers, networks and their configuration in version-controlled files so baselines are deployed repeatably and audited like software.

examTips: Know the three lifecycle words in order: establish, deploy, maintain. If a scenario describes a system drifting from its approved config, the answer is in the maintain phase.
Group Policy, Intune, Ansible and golden images are all deployment mechanisms; if the question asks how to push a baseline to many systems consistently, pick one of these over manual configuration.
CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs are external sources of baseline content; expect them to appear as the answer to how an organisation should establish a baseline without starting from scratch.
A question describing a scan that checks settings rather than vulnerabilities is describing a compliance or configuration audit, not a vulnerability scan.
videos.realWorld: In a bank SOC you will not write baselines, but you will live with them. Your SIEM will have a rule set that assumes the baseline: Windows event log forwarding on, Sysmon installed, local admin disabled. When a host stops sending logs, or a scan shows a disabled control, that is a ticket for you to triage, and part of triage is asking whether it is drift, an authorised exception, or an attacker disabling defences. GRC analysts own the baseline document itself, map each control to ISO 27001 Annex A or the CBN Risk-Based Cybersecurity Framework, and keep the exception register that auditors will ask to see.

quiz.q: A security team has adopted the CIS Benchmark for Windows Server 2022 and tailored it to the organisation. Six months later, a routine scan shows that 40 servers have SMBv1 re-enabled after a vendor installer turned it on. Which phase of baseline management has failed?
options: Maintain
Classify
Establish
Deploy
quiz.explain: The baseline was correctly established (CIS, tailored) and deployed (servers were compliant initially). The failure is that drift was not detected and corrected promptly, which is the maintain phase. Classify is not a baseline lifecycle phase.

quiz.q: An administrator needs to ensure that every new Linux virtual machine in a cloud environment starts with the approved hardened configuration, without relying on engineers to run hardening scripts afterwards. Which approach BEST meets this need?
options: Distribute a PDF hardening checklist to all engineers
Build and use a golden image that already contains the baseline
Run a vulnerability scan on each VM after it is built
Enable full-disk encryption on all VM storage
quiz.explain: A golden image bakes the baseline in so every instance starts compliant. A checklist depends on people. A vulnerability scan detects problems after the fact rather than preventing them. Encryption is a good control but does not address configuration baselines.

quiz.q: A GRC analyst is asked by an auditor to show that the organisation's database servers are hardened. Which evidence would MOST directly demonstrate this?
options: The firewall rule set protecting the database subnet
A copy of the vendor's installation manual
The most recent compliance scan results measured against the approved baseline
A list of all user accounts on the database servers
quiz.explain: Hardening is proven by comparing the live configuration to the approved baseline, which is exactly what a compliance scan report shows. The other items are useful in other contexts but do not demonstrate that the baseline is applied.

videos.title: Hardening Targets
videos.summary: Messer walks through hardening specific device types: mobile devices, workstations, network switches and routers, cloud infrastructure, servers, ICS/SCADA, embedded systems, RTOS and IoT devices.
videos.deepDive:
Hardening means reducing a system's attack surface: removing what is not needed, locking down what remains, and keeping it patched. The principle is the same everywhere, but the SY0-701 objective lists specific targets because each one has different constraints, and the exam tests whether you know those differences.

TargetWhat hardening looks likeSpecial constraint
Mobile devicesMDM enrolment, screen lock and PIN, remote wipe, disable sideloading, block jailbroken/rooted devices, app allow-listsDevices leave the building; the user often owns them
WorkstationsRemove local admin, EDR agent, disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault), disable unused services, application control, patch OS and browsersLargest population, the phishing entry point
Switches and routersChange default credentials, disable Telnet and HTTP in favour of SSH and HTTPS, disable unused ports, port security, management VLAN, SNMPv3 only, ACLs on management interfaces, firmware updatesCompromise gives an attacker the whole network
Cloud infrastructureLeast-privilege IAM roles, MFA on the root account, no public S3 buckets, security groups default deny, logging (CloudTrail) on, encrypt at rest, use CSP benchmarks (CIS AWS Foundations)Misconfiguration, not malware, is the top cloud failure
ServersMinimal install, one role per server, host firewall, disable unused services and accounts, log forwarding, patch cadence, integrity monitoringUptime pressure delays patching
ICS/SCADANetwork isolation (Purdue model), unidirectional gateways or strict firewalling, no direct internet, monitor rather than block, vendor-approved patches onlyAvailability and safety outrank confidentiality; patching may require plant shutdown
Embedded systemsFirmware updates where possible, disable debug interfaces, network segmentation, replace defaultsOften cannot be patched or run an agent
RTOSMinimal code, secure boot, restricted interfaces, vendor patchesDeterministic timing means no room for a heavy security agent
IoTChange default passwords, separate VLAN, block outbound except what is needed, firmware updates, disable UPnPCheap, numerous, rarely updated, often forgotten

Worked example: a switch. A branch office switch ships with username admin, password admin, Telnet enabled and all 48 ports active. Hardening: set a strong local password and point authentication at RADIUS/TACACS+ so admin access is tied to individual accounts; disable Telnet and enable SSH only; shut down unused ports and assign them to an unused VLAN; enable port security so a port learns a limited number of MAC addresses; move management traffic to a dedicated VLAN reachable only from the admin subnet; enable SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption and disable v1/v2c; apply the latest firmware. Now an attacker who plugs into a spare wall port gets nothing, and a phished admin password alone is not enough because access is logged per user.

The ICS/SCADA and embedded mindset. These questions catch people out. In IT we say patch fast and block by default. In a power plant or a water treatment control system, an unexpected reboot can cause physical harm, and the vendor may only certify one firmware version. So the correct answer usually involves compensating controls: isolate the network, put a firewall or data diode in front, monitor passively with an IDS, and only patch during planned maintenance windows after vendor approval. The same logic applies to ATMs and card terminals, which are effectively embedded systems running old Windows builds.

How a SOC uses this. Hardening determines what normal looks like. If routers should only accept SSH from the management subnet, then a Telnet connection attempt or an SSH login from a user VLAN is a high-fidelity alert. Analysts also feed back into hardening: after an incident, the lessons-learned report usually adds a hardening item (disable LLMNR, block Office macros from the internet, and so on).

keyTerms.def: The total set of points where an attacker could try to enter or extract data from a system; hardening exists to shrink it.
A switch feature that limits which or how many MAC addresses may use a physical port, defeating rogue devices plugged into spare ports.
A dedicated VLAN carrying only administrative traffic to network devices, reachable solely from authorised admin systems.
Industrial Control Systems and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition, the systems that run physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.
Real-Time Operating System, a minimal OS with guaranteed response timing used in embedded and safety-critical devices, which cannot host normal security agents.
A computer built into a larger device for a fixed function, often with no patching path and default credentials.
A hardware device that physically permits network traffic in only one direction, used to let ICS data out without letting attacks in.
Granting only the access needed to perform a task; the underlying principle behind removing local admin rights and tightening cloud IAM.

examTips: For ICS, SCADA, embedded and RTOS questions the answer is almost never simply patch immediately or install an agent; look for isolation, segmentation, monitoring and vendor-approved maintenance windows.
Switch and router hardening questions favour: disable Telnet, use SSH, change defaults, disable unused ports, SNMPv3, management VLAN.
Cloud hardening questions are about misconfiguration: public storage, over-privileged roles, missing MFA on the root account, and logging that is off.
If a question mentions a device with a default password that cannot be changed, the answer is network segmentation onto its own VLAN with restrictive firewall rules.
Workstation hardening: removing local administrator rights is the single highest-impact control and is a frequent correct answer.
videos.realWorld: Nigerian banks run large fleets of ATMs, POS terminals and branch switches alongside cloud workloads and thousands of laptops. A SOC analyst sees the consequences of hardening gaps daily: a branch switch still on Telnet shows up as cleartext credentials in a packet capture, an ATM on an unpatched Windows build triggers EDR alerts for a decade-old exploit, and a misconfigured S3 bucket shows up in a threat intel feed before anyone internal notices. GRC teams maintain a hardening standard per asset class and require evidence of compliance before a new system passes change advisory board review.

quiz.q: A water utility's SCADA controllers run firmware with a known critical vulnerability. The vendor has not released a certified patch and the controllers cannot run endpoint security software. Which action BEST reduces risk while keeping operations running?
options: Shut down the controllers until the vendor releases a patch
Install antivirus software on each controller
Apply the latest generic Linux kernel patch to the controllers
Isolate the controllers on a segmented network with a firewall and passive monitoring
quiz.explain: ICS devices prioritise availability and safety, and often cannot be patched or run agents. Segmentation with strict firewalling and passive monitoring is the standard compensating control. Unsupported patches or agents risk breaking the device; shutting down a water utility is not acceptable.

quiz.q: During a review, an analyst finds that a core network switch accepts management connections via Telnet from any VLAN and uses SNMPv2c with the community string public. Which set of changes BEST hardens the device?
options: Disable Telnet, enable SSH, restrict management to a dedicated VLAN, and migrate to SNMPv3
Increase the switch's log retention and enable spanning tree
Replace the switch with a router
Enable HTTP management and change the SNMP community string to private
quiz.explain: Telnet and SNMPv2c send credentials in cleartext. Replacing them with SSH and SNMPv3 (which adds authentication and encryption) and restricting management to a management VLAN directly addresses the weaknesses. Changing the community string alone still leaves cleartext SNMP.

quiz.q: A company discovers that several IoT smart TVs in meeting rooms cannot have their default administrative password changed. Which control MOST effectively limits the risk these devices pose?
options: Enrol the TVs in the corporate MDM platform
Place the TVs on an isolated VLAN with firewall rules permitting only required traffic
Install a host-based firewall on each TV
Require users to sign an acceptable use policy for the TVs
quiz.explain: When a device cannot be hardened directly, the compensating control is network segmentation so a compromise cannot reach anything valuable. Consumer TVs typically cannot be enrolled in MDM or run host firewalls, and a policy does not change the technical exposure.

videos.title: Securing Wireless and Mobile
videos.summary: Messer covers wireless site surveys and heat maps, mobile device management, the BYOD/COPE/CYOD deployment models, and the security concerns of cellular, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity.
videos.deepDive:
Wireless and mobile are grouped together in this objective because both extend your network beyond the walls you control. A cable stops at the wall socket; a radio signal does not, and a phone goes home with the employee. Securing them is therefore partly about radio planning and partly about managing devices you cannot physically reach.

Site surveys and heat maps. Before deploying Wi-Fi, an engineer walks the building with a survey tool (Ekahau, NetSpot, or even a laptop with a spectrum analyser) and records signal strength, channel usage and interference at each point. The output is a heat map: a floor plan coloured by signal strength. Security uses this in two ways. First, to place access points so coverage stays inside the building where possible and does not spill into the car park where an attacker can sit comfortably. Second, to spot rogue access points: an AP broadcasting your SSID from a location where you have no AP, or an unknown SSID with a strong signal inside your office. Periodic re-surveys are part of maintenance, because buildings and neighbouring networks change.

Mobile Device Management (MDM). MDM (Intune, Jamf, Workspace ONE, Google Endpoint Management) is the control plane for phones and tablets. Once a device is enrolled, the organisation can enforce a PIN or biometric lock, require encryption, push Wi-Fi and VPN profiles, restrict app installation, detect jailbreak or root, geofence, and remote wipe a lost device. Most MDM platforms support containerisation: a managed work profile that holds corporate email and apps, encrypted and wipeable separately from the personal photos and WhatsApp on the same phone. That separation is what makes personal devices acceptable for work.

Deployment models. The exam wants you to distinguish three.

  • BYOD (Bring Your Own Device): the employee owns it and uses it for work. Cheapest for the company, hardest to secure, raises privacy and legal questions (can you wipe someone's personal phone? what happens on termination?). Requires a signed policy and a work container.
  • COPE (Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled): the company buys and owns the device, fully manages it, but allows reasonable personal use. Strongest control; most expensive.
  • CYOD (Choose Your Own Device): the company owns it but the employee picks from an approved list. A middle ground: still corporate-owned and fully managed, but with user choice to improve adoption.

Connection methods. Each radio on a phone is a separate attack surface. Cellular is generally the most trustworthy transport, but SIM-swap fraud (very common in Nigeria, and the reason SMS-based OTP is being phased out by banks) lets an attacker take over the phone number and intercept authentication codes. Wi-Fi exposes the device to evil-twin access points and open hotspots; MDM should push a policy that requires a VPN or blocks known-bad networks. Bluetooth has a short range but supports pairing attacks (bluesnarfing steals data, bluejacking sends unsolicited messages) and is often left discoverable; a hardened policy sets it non-discoverable and limits pairing.

Worked example. A fintech allows BYOD for its sales staff. The policy: enrol in Intune, work profile only, minimum Android 13 or iOS 17, six-digit PIN, no rooted devices, corporate apps only from the managed store, Wi-Fi at branches via WPA3-Enterprise certificate pushed by MDM, Bluetooth non-discoverable. A sales rep loses her phone in Lagos traffic. She reports it, the SOC verifies her identity, triggers a selective wipe of the work profile, revokes her tokens in Entra ID, and her personal data is untouched. Without MDM the same event would be a reportable data breach under the NDPA.

The SOC connection is that MDM is a log source. Jailbreak detections, failed unlock attempts, devices that stop checking in, and geolocation anomalies all feed the SIEM and are triaged like any other alert.

keyTerms.def: A physical assessment of a building's radio environment to plan access point placement, channels and coverage.
A floor-plan visualisation of Wi-Fi signal strength produced by a site survey, used to find coverage gaps and signal leakage.
Mobile Device Management, a platform that enrols mobile devices and enforces configuration, app, encryption and remote wipe policies.
Bring Your Own Device: employees use personally owned devices for work, typically with a managed container.
Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: the organisation owns and manages the device but permits personal use.
Choose Your Own Device: the organisation owns the device but the user selects it from an approved list.
Separating corporate apps and data into an encrypted, separately wipeable partition on a mobile device.
An MDM command that erases a lost or stolen device, or just its work container, to prevent data exposure.
Unauthorised access to data on a device over a Bluetooth connection.

examTips: BYOD vs COPE vs CYOD is tested by who owns the device and who chooses it: BYOD user owns, COPE company owns and chooses, CYOD company owns but user chooses.
A heat map or site survey is the answer when the question is about wireless coverage, signal leakage outside the building, or finding interference and rogue access points.
Lost or stolen phone scenarios almost always resolve to remote wipe via MDM, with selective wipe of the container if the device is personally owned.
Jailbreaking and rooting appear as risks because they defeat OS protections and MDM policy; MDM should detect and block such devices.
Bluesnarfing (data theft) and bluejacking (unsolicited messages) are the two Bluetooth attack names to remember.
videos.realWorld: Nigerian banks are heavy mobile shops: relationship managers, field agents and executives all work from phones, and mobile banking apps are the primary customer channel. SOC analysts handle MDM alerts (a device reporting as rooted, a laptop connecting from an unexpected country, a phone that has not checked in for 30 days) and coordinate wipes for lost devices. GRC owns the BYOD policy, which must satisfy the NDPA's requirements around processing personal data on the same device as corporate data, and the CBN's expectations for securing channels used for customer transactions.

quiz.q: A company wants to standardise mobile devices for full management while still letting employees pick between an iPhone and one of two Android models. Which deployment model is being described?
options: BYOD
COPE
CYOD
VDI
quiz.explain: The company owns and fully manages the device but the employee chooses from an approved list, which is CYOD. BYOD is employee-owned. COPE is corporate-owned with the company selecting the device. VDI is virtual desktops, unrelated.

quiz.q: Users report that the Wi-Fi network is usable from the car park across the street. A penetration tester confirms she can capture handshake traffic from her car. Which action should the security team take FIRST to understand and reduce the exposure?
options: Switch all clients to Bluetooth tethering
Enable MAC address filtering
Disable SSID broadcast
Perform a wireless site survey and produce a heat map
quiz.explain: A site survey with heat map shows exactly where signal leaks and lets engineers adjust AP placement and transmit power. Hiding the SSID and MAC filtering are trivially bypassed and do not address signal leakage. Bluetooth tethering is not a network design.

quiz.q: An employee's personally owned phone, enrolled in the corporate MDM with a work container, is stolen. The employee is worried about losing family photos. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Perform a selective wipe of the corporate container and revoke the user's access tokens
Wait 24 hours to see if the phone is recovered before acting
Ask the mobile carrier to block the SIM and take no further action
Perform a full device wipe immediately
quiz.explain: Containerisation exists precisely so a BYOD device can have its corporate data removed without touching personal data. Revoking tokens prevents continued access. A full wipe destroys personal data unnecessarily; waiting leaves data exposed; blocking the SIM does not remove data from the device.

videos.title: Wireless Security Settings
videos.summary: Messer explains WPA3 and its improvements over WPA2, AAA with RADIUS, the cryptographic protocols used in Wi-Fi (GCMP, SAE), and the EAP-based authentication protocols used in enterprise wireless.
videos.deepDive:
Wireless security has two separate jobs that students often blur together: authentication (proving who may join) and encryption (protecting the frames once joined). WPA versions bundle both, but the exam tests them separately, so keep the two ideas distinct.

WPA2 and its problems. WPA2 (2004) uses AES in CCMP mode for encryption and, in personal mode, a pre-shared key (PSK) for authentication. The weakness is the four-way handshake: an attacker who captures it can run an offline dictionary attack against the passphrase at any speed their GPU allows. A weak PSK on a bank branch network is therefore a cleartext network waiting to happen. WPA2 was also hit by the 2017 KRACK attack against the handshake itself.

WPA3 (2018) fixes the handshake. In personal mode it replaces the PSK exchange with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), based on the Dragonfly key exchange. SAE is a password-authenticated key agreement: both sides prove knowledge of the password without ever transmitting anything that can be brute-forced offline. Each guess requires a live exchange with the AP, which can rate-limit. SAE also provides forward secrecy, so capturing today's traffic and later learning the password does not decrypt it. WPA3 encryption uses GCMP (Galois/Counter Mode Protocol), AES-GCM at 128 bits (192 bits in WPA3-Enterprise mode), which is faster and stronger than CCMP. WPA3 also makes Protected Management Frames mandatory, blocking deauthentication attacks used to force reconnections.

AAA and RADIUS. Personal mode shares one password among everyone, which is unworkable for an organisation: you cannot revoke one person's access without changing the key on every device. Enterprise mode instead uses 802.1X: the client (supplicant) talks to the AP (authenticator), which forwards credentials to a RADIUS server (authentication server), usually backed by Active Directory. AAA stands for Authentication (who are you), Authorisation (what may you do, which VLAN) and Accounting (log the session). RADIUS is the protocol carrying that conversation; TACACS+ is its Cisco cousin used mainly for device administration rather than network access.

Authentication protocols (EAP). 802.1X carries an EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) method, and the exam expects you to know the main variants.

MethodHow it worksNotes
EAP-TLSMutual certificate authentication: server cert and client certStrongest; requires a PKI to issue client certificates, usually via MDM
EAP-TTLSServer cert builds a TLS tunnel, client authenticates inside with password or other methodOnly the server needs a certificate
PEAPSame tunnel idea, Microsoft/Cisco/RSA design, typically MSCHAPv2 insideVery common in Windows AD environments
EAP-FASTCisco; uses a Protected Access Credential instead of a certificateLess common now

Worked example. A bank configures WPA3-Enterprise on branch Wi-Fi with EAP-TLS. The MDM pushes a client certificate to every managed laptop. An unmanaged laptop that knows a staff password still cannot join because it has no certificate; a terminated employee loses access the moment their AD account is disabled because RADIUS checks AD on every authentication; and every join is logged with username, MAC and AP, which the SOC ingests. Guest Wi-Fi is a separate SSID on an isolated VLAN, using WPA3 with a captive portal, so visitors never touch the corporate network.

For the SOC, RADIUS logs are gold: repeated authentication failures for one user suggest a stolen password being tried; a successful join from a device type you do not own suggests a certificate leak; and an AP suddenly seeing authentications for hundreds of accounts suggests an evil twin harvesting credentials. Wireless intrusion detection systems (WIDS) add detection of rogue APs and deauth floods.

keyTerms.def: The current Wi-Fi security standard, using SAE for personal authentication, GCMP encryption, forward secrecy and mandatory protected management frames.
Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, WPA3's password-authenticated key exchange that prevents offline dictionary attacks on the passphrase.
Galois/Counter Mode Protocol, the AES-GCM based encryption used by WPA3, replacing WPA2's CCMP.
The port-based network access control standard in which a supplicant authenticates through an authenticator to an authentication server before gaining network access.
Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service, the AAA protocol used by 802.1X to centralise wireless and wired authentication against a directory.
Authentication, Authorisation and Accounting: proving identity, deciding permissions, and logging the session.
An EAP method using mutual certificate authentication, the strongest common enterprise wireless method but requiring a PKI.
Protected EAP, which wraps an inner authentication (usually MSCHAPv2 passwords) inside a TLS tunnel established by a server certificate.
A property where compromise of a long-term key does not expose previously captured session traffic.

examTips: WPA3 personal equals SAE; if a question mentions preventing offline dictionary attacks on the Wi-Fi password, the answer is WPA3 or SAE.
If the scenario wants individual user accountability on Wi-Fi or the ability to revoke one user, the answer is enterprise mode with 802.1X and RADIUS, not a shared PSK.
EAP-TLS needs certificates on both sides; PEAP and EAP-TTLS need a certificate only on the server. Pick EAP-TLS when the question says strongest or mutual authentication.
GCMP is WPA3's encryption, CCMP is WPA2's; both use AES. TKIP is the old WPA1 method and is always a wrong answer for a secure configuration.
RADIUS is for network access AAA; TACACS+ is for administering network devices. Both can appear as distractors for each other.
videos.realWorld: Branch Wi-Fi at a Nigerian bank is a classic audit finding: PSKs that have not changed since installation, written on a whiteboard, shared with vendors. Moving to WPA3-Enterprise with RADIUS tied to AD fixes accountability and revocation in one step, and the RADIUS logs give the SOC a new detection source. Analysts routinely correlate a RADIUS login (which AP, which user, which time) with badge access logs to catch impossible-travel situations, and with EDR to confirm the connecting device is a managed one.

quiz.q: A penetration tester captured the WPA2 four-way handshake from a company's wireless network and cracked the passphrase offline within hours. Which change would BEST prevent this attack in future?
options: Enable MAC address filtering on the access points
Migrate the network to WPA3, which uses SAE
Reduce the DHCP lease time
Change the SSID to a non-descriptive name
quiz.explain: SAE in WPA3 is specifically designed so that captured handshake traffic cannot be used for offline password cracking. MAC filtering is bypassed by spoofing, and DHCP lease time and SSID naming have no effect on the handshake weakness.

quiz.q: An organisation wants each employee to authenticate to Wi-Fi with their own directory credentials so that access can be revoked individually when someone leaves. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: WPA3-Personal with a 32-character passphrase
WPA2-Personal with a passphrase rotated monthly
802.1X with a RADIUS server integrated with the directory
An open network protected by a captive portal
quiz.explain: 802.1X with RADIUS authenticates each user against the directory, giving per-user accountability and immediate revocation. Personal modes share one passphrase among everyone regardless of length or rotation. A captive portal on an open network provides no frame encryption.

quiz.q: A security architect requires that both the wireless client and the authentication server prove their identity with certificates before any network access is granted. Which EAP method satisfies this?
options: EAP-FAST
PEAP
EAP-TTLS
EAP-TLS
quiz.explain: EAP-TLS performs mutual certificate authentication. PEAP and EAP-TTLS use a server certificate only, with the client authenticating inside a tunnel by password. EAP-FAST uses a Protected Access Credential rather than client certificates.

videos.title: Application Security
videos.summary: Messer covers the developer-side controls in this objective: input validation, secure cookies, static code analysis, code signing, sandboxing and application monitoring.
videos.deepDive:
Most breaches of banks and fintechs today do not come through the firewall; they come through the web and mobile applications the firewall is deliberately letting traffic reach. Application security is the set of practices that make the code itself resistant to attack. The SY0-701 objective lists six, and each is a distinct exam target.

Input validation. Every piece of data arriving from outside (form fields, URL parameters, headers, API JSON, file uploads) must be treated as hostile until checked. The correct approach is allow-listing: define exactly what is acceptable (an account number is exactly ten digits, a name is letters and a few punctuation marks under 100 characters) and reject everything else. Deny-listing (blocking the characters you know are dangerous, such as <script> or a single quote) always loses because attackers find encodings you did not think of. Validation must happen server-side; client-side JavaScript checks are a convenience for users, not a security control, because an attacker sends requests directly with a tool like Burp. Input validation is the primary defence against SQL injection, cross-site scripting, command injection and buffer overflows, and is why parameterised queries (which separate code from data) are the standard fix for SQLi.

Secure cookies. Session cookies are the keys to a logged-in session, so their attributes matter. The Secure flag ensures the browser only sends the cookie over HTTPS, so it cannot be sniffed on an open network. HttpOnly stops JavaScript from reading the cookie, so even a successful XSS attack cannot steal the session. SameSite limits the cookie being sent on cross-site requests, which blunts cross-site request forgery. A worked example: a fintech's app sets Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict. A pentester finds a reflected XSS in the search box, but her payload document.cookie returns nothing useful because HttpOnly hides the session token. The bug still needs fixing, but the blast radius is far smaller.

Static code analysis (SAST). A SAST tool (SonarQube, Semgrep, Checkmarx, Fortify) reads source code without running it and flags dangerous patterns: string concatenation into a SQL query, use of a banned function, a hard-coded API key, missing output encoding. It runs in the CI pipeline so developers see findings before merge. Its limitation is false positives: it flags a pattern, not a proven exploit, so a human must triage. Its counterpart, dynamic analysis (DAST), tests the running application from outside; the exam treats both under vulnerability identification in 4.3.

Code signing. The developer signs the compiled application, script or driver with a private key; users and operating systems verify the signature with the public certificate. This proves integrity (the code was not altered since signing) and authenticity (it came from the named publisher). Windows SmartScreen, macOS Gatekeeper, and PowerShell execution policies all rely on it. Note the limit: a signature proves origin, not safety. Malware signed with a stolen certificate is still malware, which is why SOC analysts check whether a signer is expected, not merely whether a signature is valid.

Sandboxing. Running untrusted code in an isolated environment where it cannot touch the real system: browser tabs, mobile app permission models, email attachment detonation chambers, and analyst malware sandboxes (Any.Run, Joe Sandbox, Cuckoo) are all sandboxes. In development, a sandbox is a separate environment where new code is tested against production-like data without production access.

Monitoring. Applications must produce security-relevant logs (logins, failures, privilege changes, high-value transactions, input validation rejections) and those must reach the SIEM. Runtime application self-protection (RASP) and web application firewalls add live inspection. Without this, an attack on the application is invisible to the SOC until customers complain.

keyTerms.def: Checking all externally supplied data against an allow-list of acceptable values on the server before it is used.
A database query that keeps user input strictly as data rather than concatenating it into SQL, the standard defence against SQL injection.
A cookie attribute instructing the browser to send the cookie only over HTTPS connections.
A cookie attribute that prevents client-side scripts from reading the cookie, limiting session theft via XSS.
A cookie attribute restricting whether the cookie is sent with cross-site requests, mitigating CSRF.
Automated review of source code without executing it to find insecure patterns, typically run in the CI pipeline.
Digitally signing software with a publisher's private key so recipients can verify its integrity and origin.
Executing code in an isolated environment that prevents it from accessing or affecting the host system or production data.

examTips: Input validation is the answer to SQL injection, XSS, command injection and buffer overflow prevention questions; the exam prefers server-side allow-list validation over client-side or deny-list.
Cookie questions: Secure equals HTTPS only, HttpOnly equals no JavaScript access, SameSite equals CSRF protection. Match the flag to the threat described.
Static analysis reads code without running it; dynamic analysis tests the running app. A question about finding flaws before the code is compiled or deployed points to static.
Code signing proves integrity and authenticity of software, not that it is safe; a scenario about verifying an update came unaltered from the vendor is code signing.
Sandboxing is the answer when the question describes safely running or testing untrusted or new code without risk to production.
videos.realWorld: Fintech SOC analysts see application security failures as WAF alerts (SQLi and XSS signatures), as authentication anomalies in application logs, and as bug bounty reports. They also review code-signing signals in EDR: an unsigned binary or one signed by an unknown publisher running on a finance workstation is a standard hunt query. GRC and application security teams gate releases on clean SAST results and enforce secure cookie settings as a checklist item in the secure SDLC that the CBN and PCI DSS both expect a bank to operate.

quiz.q: A web application's login form is vulnerable to SQL injection. The developer proposes adding JavaScript to the page that blocks the characters ' and ; before the form is submitted. Why is this insufficient, and what should be done instead?
options: Client-side checks can be bypassed by sending requests directly; use server-side validation and parameterised queries
The characters should instead be encrypted before submission
The form should be moved to a different port
It is sufficient; browsers enforce JavaScript validation reliably
quiz.explain: An attacker never has to use the browser form; tools send crafted requests straight to the server. Validation must therefore be server-side, and parameterised queries prevent injected input from ever being interpreted as SQL. Encryption and port changes do not address the vulnerability.

quiz.q: A penetration test reveals a cross-site scripting vulnerability. While the fix is being developed, the security team wants to ensure that even a successful XSS cannot be used to steal users' session cookies. Which cookie attribute addresses this?
options: Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
Domain
quiz.explain: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript, including injected XSS payloads, from reading the cookie. Secure only restricts the cookie to HTTPS, SameSite addresses CSRF, and Domain controls scope but not script access.

quiz.q: Users of a company's internal PowerShell tools must be confident the scripts have not been modified since the security team approved them. Which control BEST provides this assurance?
options: Compressing the scripts to make them harder to read
Storing the scripts in a password-protected zip file
Signing the scripts with the organisation's code-signing certificate and enforcing an execution policy that requires signed scripts
Running static code analysis on the scripts monthly
quiz.explain: Code signing provides integrity and authenticity; a modified script fails signature verification and the execution policy blocks it. Zip passwords and obfuscation do not prove integrity at run time, and static analysis finds coding flaws rather than detecting tampering.

objectives.title: Explain the security implications of proper hardware, software, and data asset management

videos.title: Asset Management
videos.summary: Messer covers the asset lifecycle: acquisition and procurement, assignment and ownership, classification, monitoring and tracking through inventory and enumeration, and disposal including sanitisation, destruction, certification and data retention.
videos.deepDive:
You cannot protect what you do not know you have. That sentence is the whole justification for asset management, and it is why CIS Critical Security Control number 1 is inventory of enterprise assets and number 2 is inventory of software. Every other control (patching, scanning, monitoring, access control) assumes a list of things to apply it to. The SY0-701 objective walks the asset lifecycle from purchase to destruction; the exam asks about the security implication at each stage.

Acquisition and procurement. Security starts before the asset exists. Procurement should check the vendor (is the supplier legitimate, is the hardware genuine and not grey-market, does the software licence allow the intended use), route purchases through an approved process so nothing enters the environment unrecorded, and involve security in requirements: a new core-banking module must meet encryption, logging and access-control standards before the contract is signed, not after. Unapproved purchases create shadow IT: the marketing team's own cloud subscription that holds customer data no one in security knows about.

Assignment and ownership. Every asset gets an owner: a named person or role accountable for its security decisions, and often a custodian who does the day-to-day administration. Ownership is what makes accountability real. When a vulnerability scan flags a server, the ticket goes to the owner; when a laptop is missing, the owner is asked; when a system is decommissioned, the owner signs off that its data was handled correctly. Assignment to users is also recorded, so a laptop's serial number maps to a person.

Classification. Assets are labelled by the sensitivity of the data they hold and their criticality to the business. A typical scheme: public, internal, confidential, restricted. Classification drives everything downstream: a restricted database gets encryption, quarterly access reviews and a higher patch priority; a public web server holding no customer data does not need the same. For a bank, anything holding customer PII or card data is automatically high, and the NDPA and PCI DSS both effectively require classification.

Monitoring and asset tracking. The inventory is the living record of every asset with its owner, location, classification, configuration and status. It must be maintained continuously, not once a year. Enumeration is how you discover what is actually on the network to compare against the inventory: network scans (Nmap, the discovery scans in Nessus or Qualys), agent check-ins, cloud APIs listing every instance, MDM enrolment lists and switch MAC tables. The gap between enumeration and inventory is where risk hides: a device seen on the network that is not in the inventory is either a rogue device or a record-keeping failure, and both need investigating. Modern tools such as CMDBs (ServiceNow) and attack-surface management platforms automate the comparison.

Disposal and decommissioning. This is where organisations leak data most carelessly. A retired server, a returned laptop, a swapped-out ATM hard drive, an old backup tape: each holds data that the classification says must be protected, and simply deleting files does not remove it. Sanitisation removes the data so it cannot be recovered: overwriting per NIST SP 800-88 (clear), cryptographic erase (destroy the encryption key so the ciphertext is unrecoverable), or degaussing for magnetic media. Destruction physically ends the medium: shredding, pulverising, incinerating; this is required when the media will not be reused or where sanitisation cannot be verified (many SSDs). Certification is the paperwork: a certificate of destruction from the disposal vendor listing serial numbers, method and date, which the auditor will ask for. Finally, data retention policies decide what must be kept and for how long before disposal; in Nigeria the CBN requires banks to retain transaction records for years, and the NDPA requires that personal data not be kept longer than needed, so retention schedules must balance both before anything is wiped.

Worked example. A bank replaces 200 branch PCs. Inventory shows each serial, owner and classification (internal, some confidential). Drives are removed, cryptographically erased (BitLocker keys destroyed), then shredded by a certified vendor, who returns a certificate listing every serial. The inventory records each asset as disposed with a certificate reference. Six months later an auditor samples ten serials and finds each on the certificate. Compare the alternative: PCs donated to a school with drives intact, customer statements recovered with free tools, a regulatory breach notification.

keyTerms.def: The authoritative, continuously maintained record of every hardware, software and data asset with owner, location, classification and status.
Actively discovering what assets exist on the network or in cloud accounts so the result can be compared to the inventory.
The named person or role accountable for an asset's security decisions, risk acceptance and lifecycle sign-offs.
Labelling data and the assets that hold it by sensitivity and criticality so that protections can be applied proportionately.
Removing data from media so that it cannot be recovered, by overwriting, cryptographic erase or degaussing.
Sanitising encrypted media by securely destroying the encryption key, rendering the remaining ciphertext unrecoverable.
Documentation from a disposal vendor attesting which media were destroyed, when and by what method.
The rules defining how long each category of data must be kept, and when it must be disposed of, to satisfy legal and business needs.
Technology acquired and used within an organisation without approval or knowledge of IT and security, and therefore absent from the inventory.

examTips: A device found on the network that is not in the inventory is the classic enumeration scenario; the answer involves investigating it as a possible rogue asset and updating the inventory.

Sanitisation lets media be reused; destruction does not. If the question says the drives will be reused, pick an overwrite or cryptographic erase method; if it says they will be discarded, pick physical destruction with certification.
Deleting files or formatting a drive is never a correct sanitisation answer.
Classification comes before the controls: if a question asks what must be done first before deciding on protection levels, the answer is classify the data or asset.
Data retention questions balance keeping records long enough for legal or regulatory requirements against not keeping personal data longer than necessary.
videos.realWorld: In a bank SOC, the asset inventory is the first thing you open when an alert fires: who owns this host, what is on it, how critical is it, is it even ours? Alerts on unknown assets cannot be prioritised, which is why SOC teams push hard for CMDB accuracy. GRC teams own the classification scheme, run the annual asset review with owners, and keep the disposal certificates and retention schedule that CBN examiners and ISO 27001 auditors request. Attack-surface management tools that continuously enumerate internet-facing assets are increasingly a shared SOC and GRC responsibility.

quiz.q: A vulnerability scanner identifies a Linux host on the finance VLAN that does not appear in the configuration management database. What should the security analyst do FIRST?
options: Immediately power off the host
Add the host to the CMDB with a default owner
Delete the host's entry from the scanner
Investigate the host to determine its owner and purpose, and treat it as a potential rogue device until confirmed
quiz.explain: An unknown asset is a gap between enumeration and inventory and could be a rogue device or an undocumented system. Investigation comes first; adding it blindly hides the problem, deleting the scanner entry ignores it, and powering it off could disrupt a legitimate business system.

quiz.q: A company is retiring 50 laptops whose SSDs were encrypted with full-disk encryption. The laptops will be sold to a refurbisher. Which method provides reliable sanitisation while allowing the drives to be reused?
options: Cryptographic erase by securely destroying the encryption keys
Deleting the user profile folders
Formatting the drives with the operating system installer
Degaussing the SSDs
quiz.explain: Destroying the key renders all encrypted data unrecoverable while leaving the drive usable. Formatting and deleting profiles leave recoverable data. Degaussing works on magnetic media only and has no effect on SSDs.

quiz.q: During an audit, a GRC analyst is asked to prove that decommissioned database servers containing customer data were disposed of securely. Which document BEST supports this?
options: The original purchase order for the servers
The certificate of destruction listing the drive serial numbers and destruction method
The server's last vulnerability scan report
The network diagram showing where the servers were located
quiz.explain: A certificate of destruction from the disposal vendor is the formal evidence auditors expect for secure disposal. The other documents relate to earlier lifecycle stages and do not prove the data was destroyed.

objectives.title: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management

videos.title: Vulnerability Scanning
videos.summary: Messer introduces vulnerability scanning as an identification method, along with application static and dynamic analysis, package monitoring, and the concept of credentialed versus non-credentialed scans.
videos.deepDive:
Vulnerability management is the continuous cycle of finding weaknesses, deciding which matter, fixing them, and proving they are fixed. Objective 4.3 follows that cycle across five videos; this first one is about the identification methods, and the exam names several: vulnerability scanning, application analysis (static and dynamic), and package monitoring. Threat feeds, penetration tests, disclosure programs and audits are covered in the following videos.

How a vulnerability scanner works. A scanner such as Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS or Rapid7 InsightVM first discovers hosts (ping sweep, ARP, port scan), then fingerprints each one (operating system, open ports, service banners such as OpenSSH 8.2p1 or Apache/2.4.49), then compares what it found against a database of plugins, each describing a known vulnerability and how to detect it. The result is a report of findings, each tied to a CVE identifier where one exists, with a severity score, a description, and a remediation suggestion. A scanner does not exploit anything; it infers vulnerability from versions, configurations and safe probes, which is why its findings need confirmation (covered in Analyzing Vulnerabilities).

Credentialed vs non-credentialed. This distinction is heavily tested. A non-credentialed scan sees the host the way an attacker on the network would: open ports and banners only. It is fast and needs no setup, but misses everything inside the box. A credentialed (authenticated) scan logs in with a read-only account (SSH key on Linux, a domain account with WMI/SMB on Windows, or an installed agent) and inspects installed packages, patch levels, registry settings and local configuration. It finds far more, with far fewer false positives, because it reads the actual package version rather than guessing from a banner. Best practice is credentialed scans for internal assets and non-credentialed scans from the outside to see the attacker's view.

Reading a finding. A typical Nessus entry: Plugin 156032, Apache 2.4.x < 2.4.51 Multiple Vulnerabilities, Severity Critical, CVE-2021-41773 and CVE-2021-42013, Host 10.20.5.14 port 443, Output: Installed version: 2.4.49, Fixed version: 2.4.51. That tells the analyst exactly what was seen (version 2.4.49 in the banner or package list), what it is exposed to (a path traversal that led to remote code execution, actively exploited in the wild), and what fixes it (upgrade to 2.4.51). The analyst then checks whether the host is internet-facing, whether the vulnerable feature is enabled, and whether a WAF is in front of it, before deciding how urgent it is.

Application analysis. Scanners find known vulnerabilities in known software; they cannot find flaws in code your own developers wrote. That needs static analysis (SAST), which examines source code without running it, and dynamic analysis (DAST), which attacks the running application through its interface with tools like Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP, sending malicious inputs and watching responses. Static finds issues earlier and can see code paths a black-box test would never reach; dynamic finds issues that only appear with real configuration and runtime behaviour, and produces fewer false positives because it observes actual results. Mature teams run both in the CI/CD pipeline.

Package monitoring. Modern applications are mostly third-party code: a Node.js app might pull in 1,500 npm packages. Package monitoring (also called software composition analysis) tracks every dependency and alerts when a known vulnerability is published against one of them, as happened with Log4Shell in December 2021, when every organisation had to find where log4j was embedded. Tools include Dependabot, Snyk, and OWASP Dependency-Check, and the output is often a software bill of materials (SBOM).

Scan cadence and scope. Scans are scheduled (weekly for internal, daily or continuous for internet-facing), scoped by network range or asset tag, and timed to avoid disrupting fragile systems. PCI DSS requires quarterly external scans by an approved scanning vendor, which is a hard requirement for any Nigerian fintech handling card data.

keyTerms.def: A tool that discovers hosts, fingerprints their software and configuration, and reports known weaknesses matched against a plugin database without exploiting them.
A scan that authenticates to the target to inspect installed software, patches and configuration, yielding more accurate and complete results.
A scan performed without authentication, seeing only what an unauthenticated network attacker could observe.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, the standard public identifier (for example CVE-2021-44228) for a specific known vulnerability.
Examining application source code without executing it to find insecure coding patterns.
Testing a running application by sending inputs and observing behaviour to find exploitable flaws.
Tracking an application's third-party dependencies and alerting when vulnerabilities are published against them.
Software Bill of Materials, a formal list of all components and dependencies in a piece of software.

examTips: Credentialed scans give more accurate, more complete results with fewer false positives; if a question complains about missed patches or many false positives, the fix is a credentialed scan.
A non-credentialed scan is chosen when the goal is to see what an external attacker sees.
Static analysis equals source code, before running; dynamic analysis equals running application, black box. Match the wording in the question.
Package monitoring or SCA is the answer when the vulnerability is in a third-party library or dependency rather than the organisation's own code.
Vulnerability scanners identify but do not exploit; penetration tests exploit. Keep this distinction for questions asking which activity could disrupt production.
videos.realWorld: Vulnerability scanning is often the first responsibility handed to a junior SOC or security analyst at a Nigerian bank: run the weekly Nessus or Qualys scan, export the report, split it by asset owner, chase remediation tickets, and prepare the monthly metrics (critical findings older than 30 days is the number management watches). You will learn the environment faster from scan reports than from any diagram. GRC uses the same reports as evidence for CBN cybersecurity framework compliance and PCI DSS quarterly scanning requirements.

quiz.q: A security team's monthly vulnerability scan consistently reports that Windows servers are missing patches that the system administrators insist were installed. The scans run without any login credentials. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
options: The servers have a host firewall blocking the scanner; disable the firewall
The patches were not actually installed; reinstall them
The non-credentialed scan is inferring vulnerabilities from banners; switch to a credentialed scan
The scanner's plugin database is out of date; update it
quiz.explain: Without credentials the scanner guesses from service banners, which often do not change after backported patches, producing false positives. A credentialed scan reads the actual installed patch list. The other options might occasionally apply but do not explain the specific pattern described.

quiz.q: A development team wants to find security flaws in an internally built web application before it is compiled and deployed. Which identification method is MOST appropriate?
options: Penetration test of the production system
Non-credentialed vulnerability scan
Dynamic application analysis
Static code analysis
quiz.explain: Static analysis examines source code without executing it and is the only listed method that can be applied before compilation and deployment. Dynamic analysis and penetration testing need a running system; a vulnerability scanner does not analyse custom code.

quiz.q: A critical vulnerability is announced in a widely used open-source logging library. The security team needs to know immediately which of the company's 300 applications include that library. Which practice would have provided this answer?
options: Package monitoring with a software bill of materials for each application
Quarterly external vulnerability scans
Annual penetration testing
Code signing of all internal applications
quiz.explain: Package monitoring and SBOMs record every third-party dependency per application, so a new CVE against a library can be mapped to affected applications instantly. External scans and pen tests may or may not detect the library and are not timely; code signing does not track dependencies.

videos.title: Threat Intelligence
videos.summary: Messer explains threat feeds as a vulnerability identification source, covering open-source intelligence, proprietary and third-party feeds, information sharing organisations, and dark web monitoring.
videos.deepDive:
Threat intelligence is evidence-based knowledge about adversaries: who they are, what they want, how they operate, and what artefacts (indicators) their activity leaves behind. In the vulnerability management context it answers a specific question: of the thousands of CVEs published each year, which ones are attackers actually using right now, against organisations like mine? That knowledge changes priorities. A medium-severity vulnerability with a public exploit being used by a ransomware group targeting African banks matters more than a critical one with no known exploitation.

The intelligence types the exam names.

  • Open-source intelligence (OSINT): freely available information. Vendor security advisories, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue, the NVD, security researcher blogs, GitHub proof-of-concept exploits, Twitter/Mastodon infosec accounts, abuse.ch feeds of malware URLs, AlienVault OTX, and MITRE ATT&CK. Free, broad, but needs filtering; the volume is enormous and quality varies. OSINT also refers to what attackers gather about you: staff names on LinkedIn, subdomains, leaked credentials in breach dumps.
  • Proprietary and third-party feeds: commercial intelligence from vendors such as Recorded Future, Mandiant, CrowdStrike, or Group-IB, sold as a subscription. They add analyst curation, context (which group, which campaign, which sector), and machine-readable indicators delivered via STIX (the data format) over TAXII (the transport protocol) straight into a SIEM or firewall. Expensive, but the value is in relevance and speed.
  • Information-sharing organisations: ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers) are sector-specific groups where members share what they are seeing under trust agreements. FS-ISAC serves financial services globally; in Nigeria, the CBN and the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) coordinate fraud and threat information among banks, and ngCERT is the national CERT. The value of an ISAC is that an attack on one member becomes a warning for all the others within hours.
  • Dark web monitoring: watching criminal marketplaces, forums and leak sites for your organisation's name, domains, employee credentials, customer data, or insider-access offers. Services (or your own analysts with Tor and care) look for stolen bank card dumps, initial-access brokers selling VPN credentials to your network, and ransomware groups' victim listings. Finding your credentials for sale is a vulnerability identification event just as real as a scan finding.

How intelligence changes vulnerability management: a worked example. Your Nessus scan shows 1,200 high and critical findings. Your intelligence feed tells you that CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Bleed) is being exploited by LockBit affiliates and has appeared in the CISA KEV. Twelve of your findings are that CVE, on internet-facing NetScaler gateways. Those twelve jump to the top of the queue, above hundreds of theoretically more severe findings that no one is exploiting. Meanwhile, the dark web monitor reports a listing offering VPN access to a Nigerian bank; the SOC forces a password reset for all VPN users and enables MFA enforcement the same day. That is intelligence-driven vulnerability management.

Intelligence levels. Analysts distinguish strategic intelligence (trends and threat actor motivations, for executives and GRC risk assessments), operational (campaigns and TTPs, for detection engineering and hunting), and tactical (indicators of compromise such as IPs, hashes and domains, for automated blocking and SIEM matching). Tactical indicators decay fast: an attacker's IP address may be useful for days; a TTP such as living-off-the-land with PowerShell stays relevant for years, which is why the Pyramid of Pain rates behaviours as far more valuable to detect than hashes.

A SOC analyst uses threat intelligence constantly: enriching an alert (is this IP a known Cobalt Strike server?), building detection rules from new TTP reports, and running hunts when an ISAC bulletin describes a campaign targeting peer banks.

keyTerms.def: Evidence-based, contextual knowledge about adversaries and their methods used to inform defensive priorities and decisions.
Open-source intelligence: threat or target information gathered from publicly available sources.
Information Sharing and Analysis Center, a sector-specific body through which member organisations share threat information under trust agreements.
Watching criminal forums, markets and leak sites for an organisation's credentials, data or name.
An observable artefact such as an IP address, file hash or domain that suggests malicious activity.
The standard structured format (STIX) and transport protocol (TAXII) for exchanging machine-readable threat intelligence.
CISA's authoritative list of CVEs confirmed to be exploited in the wild, used to prioritise patching.
Tactics, techniques and procedures: the behavioural patterns of an adversary, catalogued in frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK.

examTips: Free and public equals OSINT; paid subscription equals proprietary or third-party feed; sector peer group equals ISAC; criminal marketplaces equals dark web monitoring. Match the scenario's wording.
If a question asks how to prioritise among many vulnerabilities, evidence of active exploitation from threat intelligence is a strong reason to move a finding to the top regardless of its CVSS score.
An organisation discovering its employee credentials for sale is a dark web monitoring scenario; the response is forced resets and MFA, not a vulnerability scan.
STIX is the format, TAXII is the transport; the exam may ask which enables automated sharing between platforms.
videos.realWorld: Bank SOCs in Nigeria consume NIBSS and CBN fraud advisories, subscribe to at least one commercial feed, and increasingly monitor the dark web for card dumps and staff credentials. A tier-1 analyst's daily enrichment of alerts against threat intel (VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, the commercial platform) is routine, and tier-2 analysts turn new intelligence reports into SIEM detection content and hunting queries. GRC uses strategic intelligence in the annual risk assessment to justify controls and budgets, and ISAC participation is itself a control that examiners look for.

quiz.q: A security manager at a bank wants early warning of attack campaigns that other banks in the same region are experiencing, shared under a confidentiality agreement. Which source BEST meets this need?
options: Open-source intelligence from vendor blogs
A financial-sector ISAC
Dark web monitoring
Internal vulnerability scan results
quiz.explain: An ISAC is specifically a trusted, sector-based sharing community where peer institutions share what they are seeing. OSINT is public and not peer-specific, dark web monitoring watches criminal sites rather than peers, and scan results are internal.

quiz.q: A vulnerability scan reports 800 findings. The security analyst has capacity to address only a fraction this week. Which additional input would MOST improve prioritisation?
options: A list of which findings have the longest description text
The total number of hosts scanned
Threat intelligence indicating which of the vulnerabilities are being actively exploited in the wild
The average age of the servers
quiz.explain: Active exploitation evidence, such as inclusion in the CISA KEV catalogue or a commercial feed's campaign reporting, is the strongest signal for what to fix first. The other options do not relate to actual risk.

quiz.q: A threat intelligence service alerts a fintech that a set of its employees' corporate email addresses and passwords appear in a credential dump being sold on a criminal forum. What is the MOST appropriate immediate response?
options: Purchase the dump to confirm its contents
Ignore the alert, since the passwords may be old
Run a full vulnerability scan of the email servers
Force password resets for the affected accounts and verify MFA is enforced
quiz.explain: Leaked credentials are an immediate account-takeover risk; resetting them and confirming MFA removes the exposure. A vulnerability scan addresses a different problem, purchasing stolen data is inappropriate, and ignoring it leaves a known risk open.

videos.title: Penetration Testing
videos.summary: Messer explains penetration testing as an identification method, the rules of engagement, and the related concepts of responsible disclosure programs, bug bounties, and system and process audits.
videos.deepDive:
A vulnerability scanner tells you a door might be unlocked. A penetration test sends a professional to try the handle, walk in, and see how far they can get. That difference, actual exploitation with a human deciding what to try next, is why pen tests find things scanners never will: chained weaknesses, business-logic flaws, weak processes, and the real-world impact of a compromise.

How a penetration test is run. Everything starts with the rules of engagement, a signed document defining scope (which IP ranges, applications, and physical sites), timing (business hours or not), techniques allowed or forbidden (no denial of service, no social engineering of named executives), emergency contacts, and how findings will be handled. Without written authorisation a pen test is a crime, which is why the exam stresses this. The tester then follows a methodology (PTES, OWASP Testing Guide, NIST SP 800-115): reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation and privilege escalation, lateral movement, and finally a report with evidence, severity, and remediation advice. Domain 5 revisits the types (known, unknown and partially known environment; offensive, defensive, physical, integrated) in the audits and assessments objective, but for 4.3 the point is that a pen test is a vulnerability identification method with higher fidelity and higher cost than scanning.

Worked example. A fintech's quarterly scan shows only medium findings on its customer portal. The annual pen test, however, discovers that the password reset function accepts a user-supplied email parameter, lets the tester reset any account's password by changing one field, and that the resulting account can then view other customers' transaction history by incrementing an account ID in the URL. Neither issue has a CVE, because they are flaws in this application's own logic. The report rates the chain critical, the developers fix both within a week, and the SOC adds a detection for rapid sequential account ID requests. Scanners cannot find this; a tester with a browser and curiosity can.

Responsible disclosure and bug bounties. Not every tester is hired. Independent researchers find vulnerabilities in public-facing systems all the time. A responsible disclosure program (also called coordinated disclosure) publishes how to report a vulnerability to you (a security.txt file, a dedicated email address), promises not to prosecute good-faith researchers, and commits to a response timeline. A bug bounty adds money: platforms such as HackerOne and Bugcrowd let you pay researchers per valid finding, with scope and rules similar to a pen test but open to thousands of testers continuously. Bounties are cost-effective because you pay only for results, but they need a mature triage team, because most submissions are duplicates, out of scope, or low value. The exam contrasts responsible disclosure (a process for receiving reports) with bug bounty (a paid incentive program), and both with an unsolicited public disclosure, where a researcher publishes the flaw without warning, which is the outcome disclosure programs exist to prevent.

System and process audits. The last identification method in the objective is the audit: a structured review of whether systems and processes match policy and standards. A system audit checks configurations, patch status and access rights against the baseline; a process audit checks whether the vulnerability management process itself works, for example whether tickets are actually closed within SLA, whether exceptions are reviewed, whether scans cover every asset in the inventory. Audits find a class of weakness that scans and pen tests miss: the control exists on paper but nobody follows it. Internal audit, external auditors (ISO 27001, PCI QSA) and regulators (CBN examiners) all perform them.

Comparing the methods. Scanning is broad, cheap, frequent and shallow. Pen testing is narrow, expensive, occasional and deep. Bug bounties are continuous and results-priced but noisy. Audits find process and compliance failures. A mature program uses all four, and the SOC is a consumer of every one: pen test reports become detection rules and tabletop scenarios, bounty reports become urgent tickets, audit findings become monitoring gaps to close.

keyTerms.def: An authorised, scoped simulation of attack in which testers actively exploit vulnerabilities to demonstrate real impact.
The signed agreement defining a penetration test's scope, timing, permitted techniques, contacts and authorisation.
A published process allowing external researchers to report vulnerabilities safely, with a commitment to respond and fix before public release.
A program that pays external researchers for valid vulnerability reports within a defined scope.
A structured review of a system's configuration, patches and access against policy and baseline.
A review of whether an operational process, such as vulnerability management, is followed and effective.
A vulnerability in how an application's workflow can be abused, which has no CVE and is typically found only by human testing.

examTips: Any pen test question involving what must exist before testing starts resolves to written authorisation and rules of engagement defining scope.
Scanner versus pen test: the scanner identifies without exploiting; the pen test exploits to prove impact and find chained or logic flaws.

Bug bounty means paying external researchers; responsible disclosure means having a defined channel and process for reports. A question about a researcher emailing about a flaw with no program in place points to the need for a disclosure policy.
An audit is the answer when the weakness is that a process is not being followed, rather than a technical flaw in a system.
Unlike a pen test, a bug bounty is continuous and pays only for valid findings.
videos.realWorld: Nigerian banks are required by the CBN framework and PCI DSS to have periodic penetration tests, and SOC analysts are usually told when one is running so they can distinguish the tester's activity from real attacks (and occasionally not told, to test the SOC itself). Analysts read the final report to build detections for the techniques that worked. Fintechs increasingly run bug bounty programs, and the SOC or application security team triages submissions. GRC schedules the tests, tracks findings to closure, and files the reports as evidence for auditors and regulators.

quiz.q: A company hires a firm to attempt to breach its customer portal. Before any testing begins, which document MUST be in place?
options: Signed rules of engagement defining scope, timing and authorisation
A bug bounty payout schedule
An updated network diagram
A vulnerability scan report from the previous quarter
quiz.explain: Rules of engagement provide the written authorisation and boundaries without which the test would be unauthorised access. The other documents may be useful but are not prerequisites.

quiz.q: A fintech wants continuous testing of its public applications by many independent researchers, paying only when a valid vulnerability is confirmed. Which approach BEST matches this goal?
options: A weekly non-credentialed vulnerability scan
A bug bounty program
An internal process audit
An annual penetration test
quiz.explain: A bug bounty program pays per validated finding and runs continuously with many testers. Annual pen tests are periodic and fixed-price, scans do not involve researchers, and a process audit reviews procedures rather than testing applications.

quiz.q: An external auditor finds that the vulnerability management policy requires critical findings to be fixed within 14 days, but half of the last quarter's critical tickets remained open for more than 60 days with no documented exceptions. What type of finding is this?
options: A false positive in the scanner
A zero-day vulnerability
A process audit finding indicating the remediation process is not being followed
A penetration test finding
